title: Processor
summary: Background work with no UI: headless isolates placed by the balancer. In the playground you add tasks, set how much CPU each one uses, and watch the balancer move them between worker pools. The file processor pushes a stream of files through processors that share the work through a consumer group, with poison, heavy and corrupt files mixed in.
try: In the playground, add a few tasks and turn their dials up until a pool's tasks add up to 80% of a core: the balancer moves the heaviest one to a pool with room.
Watch the move log at the bottom of the page: each entry gives the time, the reason, the move, and how long the task was stopped before it ran again.
Block a task twice within a minute: it goes to the quarantine pool until it has been quiet for 30 s; each further offence doubles that wait, up to 2 minutes, and a fourth keeps it apart for good.

In the file processor, raise the share of corrupt files, the dial that crashes a processor: the kernel restarts it, and the files it hadn't finished go to the other processor in its group. With the balancer, a crashed processor also goes to the quarantine. Past the restart limit (3 in 60 s by default) the kernel gives it up, and its queue grows until you press Restart on its card: set Restarts to 1 to see it sooner.

Raise the share of poison files: each one blocks its processor's loop for 2 s, which the page's 10 s kill timeout lets pass, and stalls every processor sharing its pool. A processor that blocks twice within a minute goes to the quarantine pool; when the beat can't name it, the balancer bisects instead, sending half the pool there. Its unfinished files go to the other processor in its group.

embeds.title: Playground
intro: Background work with no UI: each task is a headless isolate that keeps a share of one core busy. Add some, turn a dial up, and watch the balancer. It reads every worker's heartbeat and moves the heaviest task out of a pool that is full (its tasks add up to 80 % of a core) or stays over 50 ms of lag for 3 s. A task that blocks its loop past 100 ms twice within a minute goes to quarantine, and comes back once it has been quiet for 30 s; each further offence doubles that wait, up to 2 minutes, and a fourth keeps it apart for good.

Give a task jobs a second and its CPU dial becomes what those jobs need. The page reports each task's backlog to the balancer, which moves a task whose backlog keeps growing to where it gets more CPU. Press Calm, and a minute later quiet tasks pack back into fewer pools.

Switch a task to work after `await` and the runtime's busy time no longer sees its work. Each task also times its own work, and the page reports that to the balancer, so the card shows both: what the kernel measured, and what the task reported. Turn its report off, and the backlog is all the balancer has to go on. A task the kernel gives up on (it crashed past its restart limit) stays where it is: the balancer never moves or restarts it.

embeds.title: File processor
intro: A generator makes synthetic files at the rate you set: CSV to parse and sum, images to scale and blur, archives to compress, and data to hash with SHA-256, each more work the bigger it is. Each kind goes to its own topic, read by a consumer group of two processors, all headless isolates that share the work. A processor commits a file only once its result is out, so when the balancer moves it, what it hadn't finished goes to the group again. Poison files block a processor for 2 s, heavy ones are ten times the work, corrupt ones crash it.
With the balancer, new processors are placed at once from a declared load, which the balancer's own measurements then replace.

blocks.heading: No faults
findings: Against a worker each, the balancer runs the 8 processors on 3 workers instead of 9, with 57 MB less memory after GC and 8 points less CPU across threads. Its p95 latency is 74 ms against 39 ms.
Against one pool, it uses 1 more worker, and its p95 is 74 ms against 148 ms.
No file was lost in any run, and the kernel gave up on no processor. The balancer did 4 files twice, from the processors it moved: delivery is at least once.

blocks.firefox: Firefox: one pool falls behind, at 43.9 files a second and a p95 of 9.0 s. The balancer keeps up, at 50.1 files a second and a p95 of 94 ms, against 51 ms on a worker each.

blocks.heading: With faults
findings: In a thousand files, 2 block their processor for 2 s, 100 take ten times the work and 1 crashes it.
The balancer does about as many files a second as a worker each, on 4 workers against 9: 52.5 against 50.0, within the rounds' spread. One pool does 26.5. No file was lost.
Its latency is much higher than a worker each: a p95 of 12.7 s against 378 ms. One pool's is 20.5 s.
It did 20 files twice, where a worker each and one pool did none: a moved or crashed processor's uncommitted files go back to its group, since delivery is at least once.

blocks.heading: Faults, then calm
findings: After 60 s with faults and 5 minutes of calm, the balancer is down to 3 workers, with every processor out of the quarantine, and a p95 of 60 ms against 37 ms on a worker each.
One pool is still working through its queue, with a p95 of 89 s.
The balancer never packed its two pools into one: together they carry about a core, by the busy time the processors report, and a pool takes another only if it stays under 40 % of a core.
